query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A phase‐selective partial recrystallization treatment, implemented via heavy cold or warm working followed by a short anneal at an intermediate temperature just above the soft-phase recrystallization threshold, will refine the lamellar microstructure of as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloys in a way that simultaneously enhances both strength and ductility compared to the untreated state.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a lamellar dual-phase (soft fcc and hard B2) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a phase‐selective partial recrystallization treatment through heavy cold/warm working followed by a short anneal at a temperature just above the recrystallization threshold of the soft phase.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature mechanical loading typical of structural applications (with potential confirmation at elevated temperatures) under controlled processing parameters to ensure differential recrystallization between phases.
generation.structural_mediator: A hierarchical microstructure featuring recrystallized fine grains in the soft (fcc) phase while maintaining a continuous hard (B2) phase network.
generation.mechanism: Selective recrystallization of the soft phase increases dislocation storage and work-hardening capacity, while the continuous hard phase maintains strength. This refined microstructure reduces weak interphase boundaries and optimizes strain partitioning under load.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated samples will show a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength (e.g., exceeding the baseline true stress of ~1.2 GPa) and uniform ductility (e.g., surpassing 25% elongation) relative to as-cast or non-selectively treated alloys.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties of as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloys or those processed by non-selective thermomechanical treatments.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to diminish if the annealing exceeds the optimal temperature window (leading to full recrystallization) or if the deformation does not induce sufficient strain partitioning. Additionally, compositional variations that do not exhibit clear recrystallization thresholds between phases may not follow this trend.
generation.uncertainty: The exact processing window (ideal strain level, anneal temperature, and time) and the precise quantitative improvements in strength and ductility remain to be determined, as they can vary with alloy composition and processing equipment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set undergoes the proposed phase-selective partial recrystallization treatment (heavy cold/warm working followed by a short, controlled anneal) while the control set undergoes only conventional cold/warm working or full recrystallization annealing. Conduct comprehensive tensile tests at room temperature (and optionally elevated temperatures) and perform microstructural characterization (e.g., EBSD, TEM) to verify the presence of a selectively recrystallized soft phase embedded within an intact hard-phase network.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase identification via EBSD/TEM
Dislocation density and strain partitioning analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength and ductility compared to the baseline, and if microstructural analysis does not confirm selective recrystallization of the soft phase while retaining the hard-phase network, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. In conclusion, we proposed a universal routine of PSR to ductilize eutectic alloys. The PSR, i.e., individual recrystallization of the soft phase and recovery of the hard phase, was achieved by tailoring the strain partitioning behavior between the two phases of eutectics. Compared with traditional processing methods for eutectic alloys, the PSR prevents premature fracture by eliminating the weak boundaries and thus triggers the intrinsically superior strain hardening capacity of the two phases through dislocation multiplication and potential phase transformation. In a typical FCC/B2 EHEA, ∼35% uniform elongation and ∼2 GPa true stress were achieved. The strain partitioning-dominated PSR mechanism ensures its good adaptability in other duplex alloys, as proven in the A357 alloy. This strategy will open new frontiers of eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials in model civilization by combining their excellent castability and strengthening capacity.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) established the concept of eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) to combine a soft FCC phase and a hard B2 phase, achieving good strength and ductility. Subsequent studies (e.g., PMC5818523) refined the lamellar structure through cryo-rolling and annealing to create hierarchical microstructures, further boosting strength–ductility synergy. Research then focused on inheriting ultrafine lamellar structures via tailored thermo-mechanical processing (PMC6353877), resulting in improved strength–ductility combinations. More recently, phase-selective recrystallization (PMC9365806) demonstrated that carefully controlling recrystallization in one phase while retaining another phase’s microstructural continuity can yield high ductility at elevated strength levels. Despite these advances, fully scalable routes for robust and reproducible processing, along with predictable property control, remain challenging.
decision.unsolved: Although phase-selective recrystallization and hierarchical lamellar refinement have shown promise, the precise control of microstructural partitioning, defect density, and phase stability—particularly for different component phases—still lacks a systematic process window to achieve consistent strength–ductility gains under practical manufacturing conditions.
decision.lever: Implement a phase-selective partial recrystallization treatment (e.g., heavy cold or warm working of the as-cast EHEA followed by a short, intermediate-temperature anneal just above the soft-phase recrystallization threshold) to refine and stabilize the microstructure while preserving a continuous hard-phase network.
decision.why: Building on trends where hierarchical refinement and phase-selective recrystallization improved both strength and ductility, a carefully tuned partial recrystallization step would further optimize phase arrangement (continuity of the harder phase with a refined, ductile phase), increasing dislocation storage capacity and work-hardening potential without sacrificing ductility.
